summary:
Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, and the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under a penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report gives up to three years, and its 2022 report gives three months to three years for "carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex", with no official reports of enforcement available for that year.

Article 409 of the penal code, dated to 1973, sets three months to three years for sexual intercourse with a person of the same sex and two months to two years for an "act of lust" other than intercourse. Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending.

Under local interpretations of sharia, same-sex conduct is punishable by death. In areas controlled by al-Shabaab and in Jubaland, capital punishment is imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity, with the sentence at a judge's discretion. The 2022 State Department report records no known state-conducted executions of that kind and states that impunity generally remained the norm.

ILGA documents killings of people alleged to have engaged in same-sex activity by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed in 2024. These are raw counts; the sources give no population denominator, so the figures cannot be ranked against other jurisdictions or read as a rate. The most recent documented case in the sources is from 2024.

In government-controlled areas, civil law specifies prison sentences of up to three years and LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, as reported by the US Department of State in 2022, so no statutory complaint mechanism covers such discrimination.

The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family, which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition.

Social stigma is pervasive. Sexual orientation is a taboo topic with no public discussion in any region of the country, per US Department of State reports from 2010 and 2022, and severe societal stigma prevented LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. Human rights and LGBTQ activists and those accused of homosexuality have been forced to flee the country for fear of execution or assassination. The sources place this amid a population that is 99% Muslim and decades of civil war and unstable government.

Al-Shabaab has publicised its intent to enforce harsh punishments against homosexuality, and senior figures claimed in 2013 that a "death chamber" awaited gay and lesbian people if they returned, while UN officials nevertheless pushed for returns. The 2022 report's finding of no known state executions sits alongside that non-state threat and the general finding of impunity.

Access to care is constrained: family planning services and fact-based information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to publicly discuss HIV transmission. Since 1999 much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organisations such as the United Nations. Adult HIV prevalence was estimated at 0.5% in 2007, one of the lowest rates in Africa.
tangentialFactors:
A 2016 report by Benjamin Christman on the treatment of gay persons in Somalia, published 2 February 2016, concludes that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia because of persecution risk; it is cited as a basis for refugee-status claims and non-refoulement for LGBT asylum seekers. Al Jazeera reported in July 2013 that gay Somali refugees in Kenya faced death threats and racist discrimination, documenting persecution that drives displacement.

The archived US State Department 2010 human rights report records the conflict and al-Shabaab abuses alongside its finding of criminalisation and the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control, giving a second, older official vantage on the same legal picture.

The penalty figures in circulation differ by more than an order of magnitude, from three months to life imprisonment, and the sources do not resolve which penal code text is currently in force. Enforcement frequency is likewise unmeasured: the 2022 report states that no official reports of enforcement were available, which records an absence of reporting rather than an absence of prosecutions.
localsOnly:
Residents in government-controlled areas face prison terms of up to three years under civil law, and the sources state that LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted there. Article 410 additionally allows a security measure, usually police surveillance, to be imposed after conviction to prevent re-offending.

Severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from disclosing sexual orientation or gender identity publicly, a finding the US Department of State made in 2010 and again in 2022, with sexual orientation described as a taboo topic with no public discussion in any region. Activists and people accused of homosexuality have fled the country fearing execution or assassination.

Organised community presence is minimal: as of 2004 one group reportedly existed for LGBTQ people in Somalia, and by 2022 there were few, very discreet, mostly online-based LGBTQI+ organisations holding events. Since 1999, much of the country's AIDS/HIV education and care has been delivered by international organisations such as the United Nations, while family planning services and fact-based information on human sexuality remain hard to access.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses transgender people specifically. Nothing is sourced on legal gender recognition, gender markers on identity documents or passports, entry or visa screening, airport or checkpoint treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers, bathroom or facility rules, or access to hormone therapy and trans-specific healthcare. Any assessment of those exposures remains unresolved on this evidence.

Which penal code text currently governs is unresolved: the sources variously cite a 1964 code carrying up to life imprisonment and a 1973 code carrying up to three years, and they do not reconcile the two. Whether prosecutions occur, and how often, is likewise not sourced beyond the 2022 report's statement that no official reports of enforcement were available.

The killings attributed to al-Shabaab and other non-state armed groups are given as raw counts with no denominator and no source for a general homicide baseline in the same period, so no per-capita comparison can be made from this inventory.
